Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) [A]
Back: Layer 2 protocol that dynamically maps an IPv4 address to a 48-bit MAC address using broadcast requests and unicast replies.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Broadcast domain [A]
Back: The set of all network devices that receive a broadcast frame (FFFF.FFFF.FFFF) sent by any member; segmented by Layer 3 routers and VLANs.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) [A]
Back: IP addressing architecture allocating IP addresses without rigid class boundaries, using arbitrary bit-length prefix notation (/X).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Collision domain [A]
Back: A physical network segment where packets can collide with one another during simultaneous transmission; segmented by Layer 2 switch ports.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Default gateway [A]
Back: The IP address of the local router interface that hosts forward packets to when the destination IP resides on a remote subnet.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) [A]
Back: Client-server application protocol (UDP ports 67/68) automatically leasing IPv4 addresses and network parameters using DORA.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DNS (Domain Name System) [A]
Back: Hierarchical distributed database (UDP/TCP port 53) resolving human-readable domain names into numerical IP addresses.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

EUI-64 (Extended Unique Identifier 64) [A]
Back: Algorithmic method generating a 64-bit IPv6 interface identifier from a 48-bit MAC by inserting 0xFFFE in the middle and inverting bit 7.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Fiber optic cable [A]
Back: Physical cabling carrying data as pulses of light: Single-Mode Fiber (SMF, narrow laser core for long distances) and Multimode Fiber (MMF, LED core for campus runs).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

ICMP (Internet Control Message Protocol) [A]
Back: Network-layer protocol used for network diagnostics (ping echo request/reply) and routing error reporting (destination unreachable, TTL expired).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

IPv4 [A]
Back: Standard 32-bit internet protocol address format represented as four dotted-decimal octets (e.g. 192.168.1.1).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

IPv6 [A]
Back: Next-generation 128-bit internet protocol address format represented as eight 16-bit hexadecimal quartets separated by colons.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

MAC address [A]
Back: 48-bit hardware identifier burned into a Network Interface Card (NIC), formatted as 12 hexadecimal digits.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) [A]
Back: The largest protocol data unit (PDU) that can be forwarded across a physical network layer (default 1500 bytes for standard Ethernet).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

OSI model [A]
Back: Seven-layer theoretical framework for network communications: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

PoE (Power over Ethernet) [A]
Back: IEEE standards (802.3af 15.4W, 802.3at PoE+ 30W, 802.3bt 60W-90W) delivering DC electrical power alongside data over twisted-pair Ethernet cables.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Subnetting [A]
Back: The mathematical process of borrowing bits from the host portion of an IP address to divide a larger network into smaller, isolated broadcast domains.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) [A]
Back: Connection-oriented, reliable Transport Layer protocol providing three-way handshakes, sequencing, error recovery, and flow control.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

UDP (User Datagram Protocol) [A]
Back: Connectionless, lightweight Transport Layer protocol transmitting data with minimal overhead, without acknowledgments or retransmissions.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

VLSM (Variable Length Subnet Masking) [A]
Back: Subnetting design technique applying different subnet mask lengths to subnets of the same classful network to eliminate wasted addresses.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

802.1Q [A]
Back: IEEE standard protocol that encapsulates Ethernet frames with a 4-byte tag (including a 12-bit VLAN ID) across inter-switch trunk links.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Access port [A]
Back: A switch port assigned to a single VLAN that transmits and receives untagged Ethernet frames to connected end hosts.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

BPDU (Bridge Protocol Data Unit) [A]
Back: Management frame transmitted by Spanning Tree switches every 2 seconds to elect root bridges and prevent bridging loops.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

CDP (Cisco Discovery Protocol) [A]
Back: Proprietary Cisco Layer 2 protocol that periodically advertises device platform, software version, native VLAN, and capabilities to neighbors.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

EtherChannel [A]
Back: Link aggregation technology bundling up to eight active parallel physical Ethernet links into a single logical high-bandwidth channel.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) [A]
Back: IEEE 802.3ad / 802.1AX standard protocol that dynamically negotiates EtherChannel bundles using active and passive modes.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

LLDP (Link Layer Discovery Protocol) [A]
Back: Open IEEE 802.1AB standard neighbor discovery protocol advertising device identities and capabilities across multi-vendor equipment.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Native VLAN [A]
Back: The designated VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk that carries untagged traffic (default VLAN 1). Mismatches cause Layer 2 bridging loops.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

PAgP (Port Aggregation Protocol) [A]
Back: Cisco-proprietary protocol dynamically negotiating EtherChannel bundles using desirable and auto modes.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Port security [A]
Back: Switchport feature restricting ingress frames based on learned MAC addresses, enforcing protect, restrict, or shutdown violation actions.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

PortFast [A]
Back: Cisco spanning-tree optimization transitioning access edge ports immediately to forwarding, bypassing listening and learning states.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

RSTP (Rapid Spanning Tree Protocol) [A]
Back: IEEE 802.1w standard providing sub-second spanning-tree topology convergence using explicit handshake proposals and agreements.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

STP (Spanning Tree Protocol) [A]
Back: IEEE 802.1D standard that blocks redundant physical paths to maintain a single loop-free logical forwarding topology across Ethernet switches.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Trunk port [A]
Back: A switch interface that multiplexes traffic for multiple VLANs across a single physical link using 802.1Q encapsulation headers.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

VLAN (Virtual Local Area Network) [A]
Back: A logically segmented broadcast domain configured within physical Ethernet switches, isolating traffic at Layer 2.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Administrative distance [A]
Back: Numerical rating (0 to 255) of trustworthiness assigned to routing sources; routers choose the source with the lowest AD when routes tie.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Default route [A]
Back: A wildcard static or dynamic route (0.0.0.0/0) that forwards any packet whose destination does not match any specific route in the RIB.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Distance vector [A]
Back: Routing protocol category where routers broadcast periodic copies of their full routing tables to directly connected neighbors (routing by rumor).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Floating static route [A]
Back: A backup static route configured with an Administrative Distance higher than the primary dynamic routing protocol, activating only upon failure.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol) [A]
Back: Cisco-proprietary first-hop redundancy protocol electing one Active and one Standby router sharing a single virtual IP and MAC.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Link-state [A]
Back: Routing protocol category where routers flood Link-State Advertisements to build a synchronized topological map, running Dijkstra's SPF algorithm.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Longest prefix match [A]
Back: The mandatory forwarding rule where routers ALWAYS select the route with the most specific bit-length subnet mask (highest /X), regardless of AD.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Metric [A]
Back: A quantitative cost or weight calculated by a routing protocol to evaluate competing paths to the same destination learned from the SAME protocol.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Next hop [A]
Back: The IP address of the next router interface along the path to the packet's ultimate destination.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) [A]
Back: Open standard link-state interior gateway protocol using Dijkstra's algorithm, area hierarchies, and interface cost based on reference bandwidth.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

RIB (Routing Information Base) [A]
Back: The control plane database residing in router RAM containing all candidate routes learned by static routing and dynamic routing protocols.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Router on a stick [A]
Back: Inter-VLAN routing design using a single physical router Ethernet link configured with multiple logical 802.1Q subinterfaces.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Routing table [A]
Back: The active forwarding table on a router listing destination prefixes, next hops, metrics, administrative distances, and exit interfaces.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Static route [A]
Back: A route manually entered by an administrator that remains in the routing table as long as the exit interface or next-hop is active.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) [A]
Back: IETF open standard first-hop redundancy protocol electing one Master router and one or more Backup routers sharing a virtual gateway IP.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

CoS (Class of Service) [A]
Back: A 3-bit field inside the IEEE 802.1Q tag header used to prioritize Layer 2 Ethernet frames across trunk links (values 0 to 7).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DHCP relay [A]
Back: Router interface feature ('ip helper-address') that intercepts client broadcast DHCP Discover packets and forwards them as unicast to central servers.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DSCP (Differentiated Services Code Point) [A]
Back: A 6-bit field in the IPv4 ToS byte or IPv6 Traffic Class byte providing 64 granular Layer 3 QoS classification levels.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Dynamic NAT [A]
Back: Translates private RFC 1918 IPv4 addresses to globally routable public IPs drawn dynamically from a pool of registered public addresses.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

FTP (File Transfer Protocol) [A]
Back: Client-server application protocol utilizing TCP port 21 (control channel) and TCP port 20 (data channel) for network file transfers.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

NAT (Network Address Translation) [A]
Back: IETF standard translating private, non-routable IPv4 addresses into globally unique public IP addresses to access the Internet.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

NTP (Network Time Protocol) [A]
Back: Client-server protocol operating over UDP port 123 that synchronizes system clocks across network hardware to within milliseconds of UTC.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

PAT (Port Address Translation) [A]
Back: Network address translation with overload, mapping thousands of private IPs to a single public IP using unique Layer 4 TCP/UDP port numbers.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Policing [A]
Back: QoS traffic conditioner that enforces a hard committed rate, dropping or remarking excess packets immediately without buffering.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

QoS (Quality of Service) [A]
Back: Suite of traffic management mechanisms prioritizing latency-sensitive voice and video packets over elastic bulk data across bottlenecks.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Shaping [A]
Back: QoS traffic conditioner that buffers excess packets in memory and smooths out packet transmission rates, avoiding packet drops at the expense of delay.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) [A]
Back: Application-layer protocol using MIBs and OIDs that enables management stations to monitor device metrics and receive event traps.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Static NAT [A]
Back: A permanent, one-to-one translation mapping a single internal private IP address to a dedicated public external IP address.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Syslog [A]
Back: Standard protocol logging system messages, errors, and audit events across eight standardized severity levels (0 Emergency to 7 Debugging).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol) [A]
Back: Simple, unauthenticated file transfer protocol operating over UDP port 69, used primarily for bootstrapping and firmware backups.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) [A]
Back: Security architecture verifying who a user is (AuthN), what commands they can execute (AuthZ), and logging their actions (Acct).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

ACL (Access Control List) [A]
Back: Ordered sequence of permit and deny statements matching packet headers to permit or discard traffic at router and switch interfaces.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) [A]
Back: Security feature that intercepts ARP packets on untrusted switch ports, validating them against the DHCP Snooping database to prevent ARP poisoning.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DHCP snooping [A]
Back: Switch security feature that intercepts DHCP messages, blocking rogue DHCP servers and building an authoritative IP-to-MAC binding table.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Extended ACL [A]
Back: An ACL (numbered 100-199 or named) that filters packets by source IP, destination IP, protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP), and Layer 4 port numbers.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

IP Source Guard [A]
Back: Perimeter defense that prevents IP spoofing by matching ingress packet source IPs against the DHCP snooping binding table.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

IPsec (IP Security) [A]
Back: Open standard protocol suite that authenticates and encrypts IP packets, providing confidentiality, data integrity, and anti-replay protection.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

RADIUS [A]
Back: Open standard client-server protocol (UDP ports 1812/1813) providing centralized authentication and accounting, combining auth & authz.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Site-to-site VPN [A]
Back: Encrypted IPsec tunnel permanently interconnecting two geographically separated enterprise branch networks across the public Internet.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Standard ACL [A]
Back: An ACL (numbered 1-99 or named) that evaluates packets solely based on their source IPv4 address.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

TACACS+ [A]
Back: Cisco-proprietary client-server protocol (TCP port 49) encrypting the entire packet body and strictly separating Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

VPN (Virtual Private Network) [A]
Back: An encrypted logical network communication path established across an untrusted or public network infrastructure.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

API (Application Programming Interface) [A]
Back: A standardized programmatic software interface enabling two independent applications to exchange data and execute remote functions.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Chef [A]
Back: Configuration management automation platform using Ruby-based recipes and cookbooks operating on an agent-based pull model.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Cisco DNA Center [A]
Back: Centralized intent-based networking controller and analytics engine automating enterprise campus provisioning and assurance.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Control plane [A]
Back: The logical network plane executing routing protocols, building forwarding tables, and evaluating topology maps.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Data plane [A]
Back: The high-speed hardware forwarding plane (ASICs/CEF) that moves user packets from ingress to egress interfaces at line rate.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) [A]
Back: Lightweight text format used for data serialization and API interchange, organized into key-value pairs, objects {}, and arrays [].

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Management plane [A]
Back: The network plane handling administrative user sessions and device monitoring traffic (SSH, HTTPS, SNMP, NETCONF).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Northbound API [A]
Back: Software interface facing upwards from an SDN controller, allowing higher-level business applications and orchestration scripts to dictate intent.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Puppet [A]
Back: Configuration management tool using declarative manifests written in a custom Ruby DSL, operating on an agent-based pull model.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

REST (Representational State Transfer) [A]
Back: Architectural style for web APIs using standard HTTP verbs (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) to manage network resources represented in JSON/XML.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

SDN (Software-Defined Networking) [A]
Back: Architecture that extracts the control plane from distributed hardware switches, centralizing it into an intelligent software controller.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Southbound API [A]
Back: Software interface facing downwards from an SDN controller, used to program physical switch data planes (NETCONF, RESTCONF, OpenFlow).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

CEF (Cisco Express Forwarding) [E]
Back: Hardware IP switching architecture compiling RIB routes into FIB tables and ARP into Adjacency tables for line-rate ASIC lookups.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Control plane node [E]
Back: Fabric node in Cisco SD-Access running the LISP Map-Server/Map-Resolver database, tracking endpoint identities (EID) and locations (RLOC).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Edge node [E]
Back: Fabric switch in Cisco SD-Access connecting to wired endpoints, encapsulating client traffic into VXLAN tunnels across the campus fabric.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

FIB (Forwarding Information Base) [E]
Back: Hardware forwarding table derived from the routing table, optimized for rapid, line-rate destination IP lookups in ASIC silicon.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

GRE (Generic Routing Encapsulation) [E]
Back: Protocol (IP protocol 47) encapsulating a wide variety of network-layer protocol packets inside an IP tunnel, supporting multicast and routing updates.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) [E]
Back: Routing architecture separating an endpoint's identity (Endpoint Identifier / EID) from its current topological location (Routing Locator / RLOC).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

SDA (Software-Defined Access) [E]
Back: Cisco enterprise fabric architecture combining DNA Center, ISE, LISP, and VXLAN to provide automated, identity-based network access.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

SD-WAN [E]
Back: Software-defined wide area network fabric orchestrating multiple WAN transports dynamically using centralized policies and IPsec overlays.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

TCAM (Ternary Content Addressable Memory) [E]
Back: High-speed specialized hardware memory evaluating 0, 1, and 'don't care' (X) bits simultaneously in one clock cycle for ACL and QoS enforcement.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

vBond [E]
Back: Orchestration plane controller in Cisco SD-WAN authenticating vSmart controllers and vEdge routers and coordinating NAT traversal.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

vEdge / cEdge [E]
Back: Data plane router in Cisco SD-WAN deployed at branch perimeters, establishing secure IPsec tunnels across the WAN fabric.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

vManage [E]
Back: Centralized management plane NMS in Cisco SD-WAN providing the graphical dashboard, configuration templates, and operational telemetry.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) [E]
Back: Virtualization technology allowing multiple independent routing table instances to co-exist on a single router with overlapping subnets.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

vSmart [E]
Back: Centralized control plane engine in Cisco SD-WAN calculating best paths, enforcing business policies, and distributing encryption keys via OMP.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

VXLAN (Virtual Extensible LAN) [E]
Back: Encapsulation protocol wrapping Layer 2 Ethernet frames inside Layer 4 UDP packets (port 4789), scaling VLANs to 16 million VNIs across Layer 3.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Autonomous System (AS) [E]
Back: A collection of connected IP networks and routers managed under a single unified administrative technical administration.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) [E]
Back: The standardized path-vector exterior gateway protocol providing routing reachability across autonomous systems on the global Internet.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

BPDU guard [E]
Back: Spanning-tree protection feature that err-disables an access edge port configured with PortFast if an unauthorized BPDU frame is received.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

eBGP [E]
Back: External BGP session established between routers residing in different Autonomous Systems (default Administrative Distance 20).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

iBGP [E]
Back: Internal BGP session established between routers residing within the same Autonomous System (default Administrative Distance 200).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) [E]
Back: Communications protocol used by IPv4 hosts to report their multicast group memberships to directly connected local routers.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

MST (Multiple Spanning Tree) [E]
Back: IEEE 802.1s standard mapping dozens or hundreds of VLANs to a small number of spanning-tree instances, drastically reducing switch CPU overhead.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Multicast [E]
Back: One-to-many communication delivering a single stream of packets simultaneously to a group of interested receivers without duplicating traffic on the source.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

PIM (Protocol Independent Multicast) [E]
Back: Family of multicast routing protocols building distribution trees using existing unicast routing tables, operating in Sparse or Dense mode.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

PIM-SM (PIM Sparse Mode) [E]
Back: Multicast routing architecture assuming no downstream hosts want traffic unless explicitly requested, utilizing a Rendezvous Point (*, G) shared tree.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Rendezvous Point (RP) [E]
Back: The designated core router in PIM Sparse Mode where multicast sources register and receivers send join requests to establish shared distribution trees.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Root guard [E]
Back: Spanning-tree feature preventing an interface from becoming a root port if a superior BPDU is received, isolating rogue switches.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

802.11 [E]
Back: IEEE standard family specifying physical Layer 1 and MAC Layer 2 specifications for wireless local area network communications.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

CAPWAP [E]
Back: IETF standard protocol enabling a central WLC to manage lightweight access points over an encrypted control and data tunnel (UDP ports 5246/5247).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Centralised WLC [E]
Back: Deployment model where all AP control traffic and client data frames are tunneled back to a central controller via CAPWAP.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) [E]
Back: Authentication framework supporting multiple authentication mechanisms (EAP-TLS, PEAP, EAP-FAST) in 802.1X wireless networks.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

FlexConnect [E]
Back: Wireless AP deployment mode allowing remote branch APs to switch client data frames locally on the branch LAN if the WAN to the WLC drops.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Lightweight AP [E]
Back: An access point operating on a split-MAC architecture, handling real-time RF framing while offloading management and authentication to a WLC.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Roaming [E]
Back: The process where a wireless client moves its association from one AP to another without dropping its active network session or IP address.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

SSID (Service Set Identifier) [E]
Back: A human-readable text string (up to 32 characters) identifying a specific wireless network broadcast by access points.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

WLC (Wireless LAN Controller) [E]
Back: Central enterprise appliance responsible for RF management, security policies, client authentication, and AP firmware distribution.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

802.1X [E]
Back: IEEE standard for port-based Network Access Control using EAP to authenticate users against a central RADIUS authentication server.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

CoPP (Control Plane Policing) [E]
Back: QoS policy applied to the internal control plane interface to rate-limit traffic hitting the Route Processor, preventing CPU exhaustion DoS attacks.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

ERSPAN [E]
Back: Encapsulated Remote SPAN, wrapping mirrored Layer 2 frames in GRE headers to route packet captures across an enterprise Layer 3 network.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

IP SLA [E]
Back: Active network diagnostic feature utilizing synthetic probes (ICMP, UDP-jitter, HTTP) to measure network latency, jitter, and packet loss in real time.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

MACsec [E]
Back: IEEE 802.1AE standard encrypting and authenticating all Ethernet traffic at Layer 2 across point-to-point physical links with hardware line-rate speed.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

NetFlow [E]
Back: Network telemetry feature capturing unidirectional IP flow statistics (source, destination, ports, bytes, protocol) for security and capacity analysis.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

RSPAN [E]
Back: Remote SPAN, forwarding mirrored packets from source interfaces across intermediate switches to a destination analyzer port over a dedicated VLAN.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

SPAN (Switch Port Analyzer) [E]
Back: Local port mirroring feature copying ingress and egress packets from source ports to a dedicated packet analyzer interface on the same switch.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Streaming telemetry [E]
Back: Push-based operational data collection mechanism continuously streaming real-time metrics over gRPC/TCP subscriptions using YANG models.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

TrustSec [E]
Back: Cisco software-defined security architecture enforcing access policies using 16-bit Security Group Tags (SGTs) rather than IP ACLs.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Ansible [E]
Back: Agentless, open-source automation engine executing declarative idempotent tasks defined in human-readable YAML playbooks over SSH.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

EEM (Embedded Event Manager) [E]
Back: On-box Cisco automation system triggering automated CLI remediations and syslogs in response to system events and regex patterns.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

NETCONF [E]
Back: IETF network management protocol using SSH (port 830) and XML RPCs to install, manipulate, and query configuration and state data.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

RESTCONF [E]
Back: IETF protocol providing programmatic access to network configuration and operational data modeled in YANG using HTTP and JSON/XML.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

YANG [E]
Back: Data modeling language (RFC 6020) defining the schema, hierarchy, types, and constraints of data manipulated by NETCONF and RESTCONF.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

BGP attributes [R]
Back: Parameters attached to BGP routes (Weight, Local Pref, AS-Path, Origin, MED) governing the 13-step best path selection algorithm.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

BGP community [R]
Back: Numerical tag (formatted as ASN:nn) attached to BGP routes used to group destinations and trigger upstream traffic policies.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Distribute list [R]
Back: Filtering tool applying an ACL or prefix list directly to a routing protocol to suppress specific inbound or outbound route advertisements.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm) [R]
Back: Finite state machine algorithm used by EIGRP guaranteeing mathematically loop-free alternate paths without periodic SPF recalculations.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

EIGRP named mode [R]
Back: Unified hierarchical configuration mode for EIGRP organizing all settings into clean address families (IPv4/IPv6) and af-interfaces.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Feasible successor [R]
Back: A backup next-hop router in EIGRP whose Advertised Distance (AD) is strictly less than the current Feasible Distance (FD) of the Successor.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

LSA (Link-State Advertisement) [R]
Back: Data packet used by OSPF to flood topological information throughout an area, categorized into Types 1 through 5, and Type 7.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

MP-BGP (Multiprotocol BGP) [R]
Back: BGP extensions supporting multiple network-layer protocols, including native IPv6, MPLS VPNv4, and EVPN address families.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

NSSA (Not-So-Stubby Area) [R]
Back: An OSPF stub area permitting local ASBRs to inject external routes via Type 7 LSAs, which are translated to Type 5 by the ABR.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

PBR (Policy-Based Routing) [R]
Back: Mechanism overriding the standard destination-based routing table using route-map match criteria to forward packets based on source or protocol.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Prefix list [R]
Back: High-performance route filtering tool evaluating IP prefixes and subnet mask lengths using greater-than (ge) and less-than (le) qualifiers.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Route map [R]
Back: Modular programming tool applying conditional match statements and set actions to filter routes or modify routing protocol metrics.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Route reflector [R]
Back: BGP router configured to reflect iBGP-learned routes to other internal peers, eliminating the scalability requirement for a full iBGP mesh.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Route tag [R]
Back: A 32-bit integer attached to a route used to identify its origin and prevent mutual redistribution feedback loops across boundaries.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Stub area [R]
Back: An OSPF area blocking external Type 5 LSAs, replacing them with a single default route injected by the Area Border Router (ABR).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

DMVPN (Dynamic Multipoint VPN) [R]
Back: Cisco solution combining mGRE, NHRP, and IPsec to build dynamic, on-demand spoke-to-spoke encrypted VPN meshes over any IP underlay.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

FlexVPN [R]
Back: Unified Cisco VPN framework built entirely on IKEv2 supporting remote access, site-to-site, and hub-and-spoke using Virtual Tunnel Interfaces (VTIs).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

IKE (Internet Key Exchange) [R]
Back: Protocol managing authentication, security associations, and key generation for IPsec (IKEv1 legacy and IKEv2 modern).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Label [R]
Back: A 20-bit identifier placed in an MPLS shim header between Layer 2 and Layer 3 used for high-speed packet forwarding without IP lookups.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

LDP (Label Distribution Protocol) [R]
Back: Protocol used by MPLS routers to exchange label-to-prefix binding information across a provider network.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

LFIB (Label Forwarding Information Base) [R]
Back: Hardware table used by MPLS routers to swap, push, or pop labels on incoming packets at line rate.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

mGRE (Multipoint GRE) [R]
Back: Tunnel interface allowing a single GRE tunnel to communicate with multiple dynamic endpoints via NHRP resolution.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) [R]
Back: High-performance packet-forwarding technology using short 20-bit labels instead of long routing table lookups.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

MPLS Layer 3 VPN [R]
Back: Service provider architecture delivering isolated customer routing domains across an MPLS core using VRFs, RDs, RTs, and MP-BGP.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

NHRP (Next Hop Resolution Protocol) [R]
Back: Protocol used in DMVPN to map dynamic public NBMA IP addresses to static virtual tunnel IPs, enabling spoke-to-spoke shortcuts.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Route Distinguisher (RD) [R]
Back: An 8-byte prefix prepended to an IPv4 address to make it globally unique across an MPLS VPNv4 network.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Route Target (RT) [R]
Back: An 8-byte BGP extended community specifying which customer VRF routing tables import and export specific routes.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

VPNv4 [R]
Back: A 12-byte address format combining an 8-byte Route Distinguisher with a 4-byte IPv4 address in MP-BGP.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Control plane [R]
Back: The router plane managing routing protocol packets, network discovery, and device control traffic.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Data plane [R]
Back: The high-speed router plane forwarding user data packets from ingress to egress interfaces.

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

Management plane [R]
Back: The plane handling administrative user sessions, CLI configuration, and monitoring traffic (SSH, SNMP).

Front:
What is the definition and operational role of:

uRPF (Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding) [R]
Back: Security feature mitigating IP spoofing by checking whether packet source IPs match active reverse FIB paths (Strict or Loose mode).

[Chapter 1 Practice Question 1.1]

Which network topology architecture replaces traditional spanning-tree blocking in modern leaf-spine data centers by providing non-blocking, predictable east-west traffic flows?

• A. Three-Tier Core-Distribution-Access
• B. Collapsed Core
• C. Clos / Spine-Leaf Architecture
• D. Hub-and-Spoke WAN
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Spine-leaf (Clos) architecture connects every leaf switch to every spine switch, utilizing ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Pathing) at Layer 3 rather than STP at Layer 2 to provide predictable latency and eliminate link blocking.

[Chapter 1 Practice Question 1.2]

A network host assigns itself the IPv4 address 169.254.11.89 with a /16 subnet mask. What does this indicate?

• A. The host obtained an address from an authoritative public DHCP server.
• B. The host failed to receive a response to its DHCP Discover and assigned an APIPA address.
• C. The default gateway statically assigned a link-local IPv4 management IP.
• D. The host has an IP conflict on the local collision domain.
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The range 169.254.0.0/16 is reserved for Automatic Private IP Addressing (APIPA). Operating systems assign an APIPA address when a DHCP client sends Discover messages but receives no DHCP Offer.

[Chapter 1 Practice Question 1.3]

What is the primary operational difference between a Type 1 and a Type 2 hypervisor?

• A. Type 1 hypervisors run directly on bare-metal hardware; Type 2 hypervisors run as software atop an existing host OS.
• B. Type 1 hypervisors only support Linux guests; Type 2 only supports Windows.

Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Type 1 hypervisors (e.g., VMware ESXi, Cisco HyperFlex) install directly on bare-metal server hardware for high performance, whereas Type 2 hypervisors (e.g., VMware Workstation, VirtualBox) execute within a host operating system.

Which command on a Windows endpoint displays the active IPv4 address, subnet mask, default gateway, and DNS servers?

• B. ip addr show

[Chapter 1 Practice Question 1.5]

What happens when an Ethernet switch receives a frame destined for an unknown unicast MAC address?

• A. The switch drops the frame immediately.
• B. The switch sends an ICMP destination unreachable message back to the sender.
• C. The switch floods the frame out all ports within the ingress VLAN except the receiving port.
• D. The switch buffers the frame and queries the DNS server.
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: When a destination MAC address is not found in the CAM table (unknown unicast), the switch floods the frame out all active interfaces in the same broadcast domain (VLAN), excluding the port on which it arrived.

In 802.1Q trunking, what happens to frames transmitted across the trunk that belong to the native VLAN?

What is the result of configuring 'channel-group 1 mode desirable' on Switch-A and 'channel-group 1 mode auto' on Switch-B?

Which Spanning Tree feature immediately transitions an access port from blocking to forwarding while bypassing listening and learning?

• B. Root Guard

[Chapter 3 Practice Question 3.1]

A router has four routes to 10.1.1.0 in its routing table: OSPF (10.1.1.0/24 AD 110), EIGRP (10.1.0.0/16 AD 90), BGP (10.1.1.0/26 AD 20), and a Static Route (10.0.0.0/8 AD 1). A packet arrives destined for 10.1.1.15. Which route is chosen for forwarding?

• B. EIGRP because AD 90 is lower than OSPF.
• C. BGP because 10.1.1.0/26 has the longest prefix match (/26).
• D. OSPF because /24 is standard class C.
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Routers ALWAYS evaluate the Longest Prefix Match (LPM) first before ever considering Administrative Distance. The /26 route has the most specific bit match (26 bits vs 24, 16, 8), so it is selected regardless of AD.

What is the purpose of configuring an administrative distance of 254 on a static route when a dynamic routing protocol with AD 110 is active?

• B. It creates a floating static route that only enters the routing table if the primary dynamic route fails.
• C. It prevents routing loops by poisoning the static route.

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: A floating static route is assigned an administrative distance higher than the primary dynamic routing protocol. It remains dormant until the primary route drops out of the RIB.

• C. The MAC address of the first GigabitEthernet interface.
• D. The IP address of the default gateway.
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: OSPF RID selection order: (1) manual 'router-id' command, (2) highest IPv4 address on active loopback interfaces, (3) highest IPv4 address on active physical interfaces (in 'up/up' state).

What virtual MAC address format does HSRP version 1 use for group 10?

Two routers fail to form an OSPF adjacency and remain stuck in the EXSTART state. What is the most common cause?

• A. Subnet mask mismatch.
• B. Interface MTU mismatch.
• C. Area ID mismatch.

[Chapter 4 Practice Question 4.4]

What is the key functional difference between Traffic Policing and Traffic Shaping?

• A. Policing buffers excess packets; Shaping drops them.
• B. Policing drops or remarks excess traffic immediately exceeding the CIR; Shaping buffers excess traffic to smooth transmission rates.
• C. Policing operates only at Layer 2; Shaping operates only at Layer 3.
• D. Policing increases bandwidth; Shaping decreases latency.
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Traffic policing enforces a hard bandwidth rate by discarding or remarking excess packets with zero added delay. Traffic shaping buffers excess packets into a queue and releases them smoothly over time, introducing queuing delay.

[Chapter 4 Practice Question 4.5]

Which stratum level indicates an NTP server directly connected to a high-precision atomic clock or GPS reference source?

• B. Stratum 1
• C. Stratum 2

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Stratum 0 is the physical reference clock itself (GPS/atomic). A Stratum 1 server is directly synchronized to a Stratum 0 clock. Stratum 16 represents an unsynchronized/unreachable device.

Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) relies on which database to validate ARP reply packets on untrusted switch ports?

Back:

What key exchange mechanism makes WPA3 Personal immune to offline dictionary attacks even if a user chooses a weak pre-shared password?

Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: vBond is the orchestrator. It authenticates vSmart controllers, vManage instances, and vEdge routers, coordinating initial connectivity and NAT traversal so devices can join the SD-WAN overlay fabric.

Front:
[Chapter 7 Practice Question 7.2]

What protocol is used to encapsulate Layer 2 Ethernet frames across a Layer 3 underlay IP network using UDP port 4789 in VXLAN fabric environments?

• A. GRE
• B. VXLAN
• C. IPsec
• D. MPLS
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Virtual Extensible LAN (VXLAN) encapsulates Layer 2 frames within UDP packets (destination port 4789), allowing up to 16 million virtual network identifiers (VNIs) to run across an arbitrary Layer 3 IP underlay.

Front:
[Chapter 7 Practice Question 7.3]

What is the primary difference between Cisco Express Forwarding (CEF) and legacy process switching on enterprise routers?

• A. Process switching caches routes; CEF queries the route table per frame.
• B. CEF pre-computes forwarding lookups into hardware-ready Forwarding Information Base (FIB) and Adjacency tables, bypassing the CPU.
• C. Process switching uses TCAM; CEF runs entirely in software.
• D. CEF only works with static routing.
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: CEF optimizes forwarding by pre-building the FIB (derived from the routing table) and the Adjacency table (derived from the ARP table). Packets are forwarded in hardware ASIC line rate without CPU interruption.

Front:
[Chapter 7 Practice Question 7.4]

Which cloud computing service model provides customers with virtual machines, raw compute, storage, and networking hardware while leaving OS management and patching to the customer?

• A. Software as a Service (SaaS)
• B. Platform as a Service (PaaS)
• C. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
• D. Function as a Service (FaaS)
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: In IaaS (e.g., AWS EC2, Azure VMs), the cloud vendor provides hypervisors, physical storage, and networking; the customer is responsible for installing, configuring, and maintaining the operating system and applications.

Front:
[Chapter 7 Practice Question 7.5]

What high-availability technology maintains active control plane synchronization between dual supervisors, enabling sub-second switchover without neighbor adjacency drops via Non-Stop Forwarding (NSF)?

• A. HSRP
• B. Stateful Switchover (SSO)
• C. VSS
• D. LACP
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Stateful Switchover (SSO) continuously synchronizes state and protocol databases between active and standby supervisor engines. Combined with NSF/Graceful Restart, it prevents routing peers from resetting adjacencies during failover.

Front:
[Chapter 8 Practice Question 8.1]

Which BGP path attribute is Cisco-proprietary, local to the router, has highest priority in decision making, and is NEVER advertised to BGP peers?

• A. Local Preference
• B. Weight
• C. AS-Path
• D. Multi-Exit Discriminator (MED)
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Weight is a 16-bit integer (0–65535, default 32768 for locally originated routes, 0 for learned routes) local to the router. It is the very first attribute checked in Cisco BGP path selection and is never propagated in BGP UPDATE packets.

Front:
[Chapter 8 Practice Question 8.2]

What is the default value of BGP Local Preference, and in what direction does it influence traffic?

• A. Default 100; influences outbound traffic leaving the Autonomous System.
• B. Default 0; influences inbound traffic entering the Autonomous System.
• C. Default 32768; influences only local router forwarding.
• D. Default 500; influences eBGP peer selection.
Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Local Preference defaults to 100, is exchanged throughout the internal AS via iBGP, and influences OUTBOUND traffic flow (higher is preferred). MED influences inbound traffic.

Front:
[Chapter 8 Practice Question 8.3]

In Multiple Spanning Tree Protocol (MSTP, IEEE 802.1s), how are VLANs handled to reduce switch CPU overhead compared to PVST+?

• A. Each VLAN runs its own independent spanning-tree instance.
• B. Multiple VLANs are mapped to a smaller number of consolidated MST instances (MSTIs).
• C. Spanning tree is disabled and replaced by shortest path bridging.
• D. Only VLAN 1 runs spanning tree; other VLANs are unmanaged.
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: MSTP maps dozens or hundreds of VLANs to a handful of MST instances (e.g., 2 or 3 instances for forwarding load balancing), drastically reducing BPDU generation and switch CPU overhead.

Front:
[Chapter 8 Practice Question 8.4]

Which PIM mode relies on a Rendezvous Point (RP) where multicast senders register and receivers join shared trees (*, G)?

• A. PIM Dense Mode
• B. PIM Sparse Mode
• C. PIM Source-Specific Multicast (SSM)
• D. Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: PIM Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) assumes no downstream hosts want multicast traffic unless explicitly requested. Receivers join the shared tree rooted at the Rendezvous Point (RP) via (*, G) joins.

Front:
[Chapter 8 Practice Question 8.5]

What switch feature automatically disables a port if an unauthorized BPDU is received on an edge port with PortFast enabled?

• A. Root Guard
• B. Loop Guard
• C. BPDU Guard
• D. Storm Control
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: BPDU Guard protects the spanning-tree topology. If an edge port configured with PortFast receives any BPDU (indicating an unauthorized switch was connected), BPDU Guard puts the port into err-disabled state.

Front:
[Chapter 9 Practice Question 9.1]

In an enterprise wireless deployment, what is the term for a client roaming between two Access Points connected to the same Wireless LAN Controller without changing IP address or subnet?

• A. Inter-controller Layer 3 Roam
• B. Intra-controller Layer 2 Roam
• C. BSSID Inter-VLAN Transition
• D. CAPWAP Asymmetric Tunnel
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: An intra-controller Layer 2 roam occurs when a wireless client moves between two APs managed by the same WLC on the same VLAN/subnet. The client maintains its IP address and session without mobility tunnels.

Front:
[Chapter 9 Practice Question 9.2]

Which wireless location tracking mechanism calculates client position by measuring the Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) from at least three separate Access Points?

• A. Angle of Arrival (AoA)
• B. Time Difference of Arrival (TDoA)
• C. Trilateration / RF Fingerprinting
• D. GPS Geofencing
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: Trilateration uses the RSSI (signal strength) reported by three or more Access Points, cross-referencing signal decay against an RF floor plan to pinpoint client coordinates.

Front:
[Chapter 9 Practice Question 9.3]

Which AP deployment mode allows a lightweight AP at a remote branch to switch client data frames locally on the branch switch if WAN connectivity to the central WLC is lost?

• A. Local Mode
• B. FlexConnect Mode
• C. Sniffer Mode
• D. Bridge Mode
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: FlexConnect (formerly H-REAP) allows access points in branch offices to locally switch client data traffic on the branch LAN without backhauling across the WAN to the central WLC, even during WAN outages.

Front:
[Chapter 9 Practice Question 9.4]

Which EAP authentication method uses a server-side digital certificate to establish an encrypted TLS tunnel inside which user credentials are validated using MS-CHAPv2?

• A. EAP-TLS
• B. PEAP (Protected EAP)

Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: PEAP only requires a digital certificate installed on the RADIUS authentication server (e.g., Cisco ISE). It creates an encrypted TLS tunnel and authenticates clients using password-based MS-CHAPv2, eliminating client certificate management.

Front:
[Chapter 9 Practice Question 9.5]

What 802.11 standard amendment enables Fast BSS Transition (FT) to minimize authentication latency during client roaming in enterprise 802.1X networks?

• A. 802.11k
• B. 802.11v
• C. 802.11r
• D. 802.11w
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: IEEE 802.11r (Fast BSS Transition) caches authentication keys across APs, allowing 802.1X clients to roam between APs in under 50 ms without undergoing a full 4-way EAP reauthentication, preventing VoIP drops.

Front:
[Chapter 10 Practice Question 10.1]

Which diagnostic utility mirrors mirrored traffic from multiple source ports across a routed Layer 3 IP network by encapsulating frames in GRE packets?

• A. Local SPAN
• B. Remote SPAN (RSPAN)
• C. Encapsulated Remote SPAN (ERSPAN)
• D. NetFlow v9
Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: ERSPAN (Encapsulated Remote SPAN) encapsulates mirrored Layer 2 traffic inside a GRE tunnel (IP protocol 47), routing packet captures across any enterprise Layer 3 network to a remote packet analyzer.

Front:
[Chapter 10 Practice Question 10.2]

What is the primary difference between traditional SNMP polling and Model-Driven Streaming Telemetry in network monitoring?

• A. SNMP operates in real-time; telemetry polls every 5 minutes.
• B. SNMP pulls data periodically via CPU-heavy polling; streaming telemetry continuously pushes granular operational data subscriptions via gRPC/TCP.

Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Streaming telemetry replaces pull-based SNMP polling with a push-based subscription model. Switches continuously stream requested data models (YANG) over high-performance gRPC/TCP transport with minimal CPU impact.

Front:
[Chapter 10 Practice Question 10.3]

In Cisco TrustSec, what 16-bit metadata value is inserted into the Layer 2 Ethernet frame header to enforce role-based access policies regardless of IP address?

• A. Security Group Tag (SGT)
• B. Virtual Network Identifier (VNI)
• C. DSCP Field
• D. MPLS Label
Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: Cisco TrustSec assigns an SGT (Security Group Tag) to packets at ingress based on authenticated user identity. Downstream switches enforce Security Group ACLs (SGACLs) using this SGT, decoupling security from IP addressing.

Front:
[Chapter 10 Practice Question 10.4]

Which IP SLA measurement tracks continuous network latency and jitter to determine if VoIP call quality meets enterprise Service Level Agreements?

• A. icmp-echo
• B. udp-jitter
• C. tcp-connect
• D. http get
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The 'udp-jitter' IP SLA probe generates synthetic UDP streams with timestamps to accurately measure one-way latency, round-trip delay, packet jitter, and packet loss for voice/video engineering.

[Chapter 10 Practice Question 10.5]

Which Syslog severity level corresponds to 'Critical' conditions requiring immediate attention?

• A. Level 0
• B. Level 2

Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Syslog levels: 0 = Emergency, 1 = Alert, 2 = Critical, 3 = Error, 4 = Warning, 5 = Notice, 6 = Informational, 7 = Debugging.

[Chapter 11 Practice Question 11.1]

In Python network automation, what is the purpose of the 'netmiko' library?

Explanation: Netmiko is an open-source Python library built on Paramiko that provides optimized SSH handling, prompt detection, and command execution across Cisco IOS, IOS-XE, NX-OS, and other networking platforms.

[Chapter 11 Practice Question 11.2]

What data modeling language is standardized in RFC 6020 to formally describe network configurations and operational state accessed by NETCONF and RESTCONF?

• B. JSON

Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: YANG (Yet Another Next Generation) is the standardized data modeling language used to define the schema, hierarchy, types, and constraints of data manipulated by NETCONF and RESTCONF.

[Chapter 11 Practice Question 11.3]

Which Cisco IOS-XE automation feature allows engineers to trigger local actions (such as generating syslogs or executing CLI commands) in response to specific system events without an external controller?

• B. Embedded Event Manager (EEM)
• C. Guest Shell Python
• D. IP SLA Tracking
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Cisco Embedded Event Manager (EEM) provides on-box automation applets that monitor system events (syslog triggers, interface state changes, timers) and execute automated CLI remediations.

[Chapter 11 Practice Question 11.4]

What transport protocol and default TCP port does NETCONF use for secure device configuration exchange?

• B. HTTPS on TCP port 443

Back:
Correct Answer: C

Explanation: NETCONF operates over an encrypted SSH session on standardized TCP port 830, exchanging XML-formatted Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs).

[Chapter 11 Practice Question 11.5]

What RESTCONF HTTP verb corresponds to retrieving configuration or operational state modeled by YANG?

• B. GET

Explanation: In RESTCONF, the GET method retrieves data from the device datastore (`/restconf/data/...`). POST creates resources, PUT replaces, PATCH partially updates, and DELETE deletes.

[Chapter 12 Practice Question 12.1]

When redistributing routes between OSPF and EIGRP, what must be explicitly configured under EIGRP for the redistributed routes to enter the routing table?

Correct Answer: B

Explanation: EIGRP considers routes redistributed from other protocols to have an infinite (unreachable) metric unless default metric components (bandwidth, delay, reliability, load, MTU) are specified via the 'default-metric' command or in a route-map.

Front:
[Chapter 12 Practice Question 12.2]

Which OSPF LSA Type is generated by an Autonomous System Boundary Router (ASBR) to inject external routes into a standard OSPF area?

• A. Type 1 Router LSA
• B. Type 3 Summary LSA
• C. Type 4 ASBR Summary LSA
• D. Type 5 External LSA
Back:
Correct Answer: D

Explanation: Type 5 External LSAs are originated by ASBRs to advertise external routes across an entire OSPF domain. Type 4 LSAs are generated by ABRs to inform other areas how to reach the ASBR.

Front:
[Chapter 12 Practice Question 12.3]

What tool in Policy-Based Routing (PBR) matches incoming packet attributes and specifies an alternate next-hop forwarding address, bypassing the standard routing table?

• A. Prefix-list applied to an interface

• C. Distribute-list applied under 'router bgp'
• D. IP SLA probe tracking default gateway
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: PBR uses a route-map applied to an ingress interface using the 'ip policy route-map' command. Traffic matching ACL criteria is steered toward a specific next-hop specified by 'set ip next-hop'.

Front:
[Chapter 12 Practice Question 12.4]

In EIGRP Named Mode, where are interface-specific parameters such as authentication, hello intervals, and split-horizon configured?

• B. Under the 'af-interface' submode inside the address-family.
• C. In the global configuration mode.
• D. In a route-map assigned to the EIGRP process.
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: EIGRP Named Mode consolidates all settings into hierarchical submodes under 'router eigrp '. Interface settings are cleanly configured under 'address-family ipv4 unicast' -> 'af-interface '.

Front:
[Chapter 12 Practice Question 12.5]

Why is an iBGP Route Reflector (RR) deployed in large enterprise Autonomous Systems?

• A. To overcome the iBGP full-mesh requirement without modifying BGP loop prevention rules.
• B. To encrypt BGP payloads across public Internet links.
• C. To allow eBGP peers to share the same AS number.
• D. To increase BGP convergence time.
Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: By default, iBGP routers do not re-advertise routes learned from an iBGP peer to other iBGP peers (iBGP split-horizon), requiring a full mesh of peerings. A Route Reflector reflects routes between clients, eliminating full-mesh scalability issues.

Front:
[Chapter 13 Practice Question 13.1]

In DMVPN Phase 3, what protocol message is sent by a spoke router to request an on-demand shortcut tunnel directly to another spoke?

• A. NHRP Resolution Request
• B. OSPF Hello Broadcast
• C. BGP Update with MED
• D. IPsec Phase 1 Proposal
Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: In DMVPN Phase 3, when traffic traverses the hub, the hub sends an NHRP Redirect to the spoke. The spoke then transmits an NHRP Resolution Request to find the target spoke's public NBMA IP and build a direct spoke-to-spoke tunnel.

Front:
[Chapter 13 Practice Question 13.2]

In an MPLS Layer 3 VPN network, what BGP mechanism is used by Provider Edge (PE) routers to separate overlapping customer subnets and route targets?

Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: MP-BGP prepends an 8-byte Route Distinguisher (RD) to customer 32-bit IPv4 prefixes to create globally unique 96-bit VPNv4 addresses. Route Targets (RTs) control route import/export into customer VRF routing tables.

Front:
[Chapter 13 Practice Question 13.3]

What is the key enhancement provided by FlexVPN compared to legacy Cisco Easy VPN and crypto maps?

• B. FlexVPN uses IKEv2 as a unified framework supporting site-to-site, remote access, and spoke-to-spoke tunnels with VTI interfaces.

Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: FlexVPN unifies all VPN topologies (point-to-point, remote access, DMVPN) into a single framework based on IKEv2 and Virtual Tunnel Interfaces (VTIs), simplifying configuration and supporting IPv4/IPv6 natively.

Front:
[Chapter 13 Practice Question 13.4]

What component of an MPLS label specifies the Quality of Service / Class of Service marking in the label header?

• A. 20-bit Label Field
• B. 3-bit Traffic Class (formerly EXP bits)
• C. 1-bit Bottom-of-Stack (S) bit

Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: The 3-bit Traffic Class (TC) field (formerly experimental bits / EXP) in the MPLS shim header carries DiffServ QoS markings across the service provider core.

Front:
[Chapter 13 Practice Question 13.5]

In DMVPN configurations, what command must be configured on the hub router's mGRE tunnel interface to enable Phase 3 shortcut routing?

• A. ip nhrp redirect
• B. ip nhrp shortcut
• C. ip ospf network point-to-point

Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: On the DMVPN hub, 'ip nhrp redirect' instructs the hub to signal spokes that a direct path exists. On the spokes, 'ip nhrp shortcut' enables them to rewrite the CEF forwarding path once the resolution completes.

Front:
[Chapter 14 Practice Question 14.1]

What security mechanism protects a Cisco router's CPU from distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) exhaustion attacks by rate-limiting control plane traffic using Modular QoS CLI (MQC)?

• B. Control Plane Policing (CoPP)
• C. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI)
• D. Port Security
Back:
Correct Answer: B

Explanation: Control Plane Policing (CoPP) treats traffic destined for the router's Route Processor as a special control plane interface, applying MQC policing filters to drop excessive management/control packets before they exhaust CPU cycles.

Front:
[Chapter 14 Practice Question 14.2]

What is the difference between Unicast Reverse Path Forwarding (uRPF) Strict Mode and Loose Mode?

• A. Strict mode requires a route in the FIB and arrival on the specific best matching interface; Loose mode only checks if any route to the source IP exists in the FIB.

• C. Strict mode drops all broadcast packets; Loose mode drops unicast.

Back:
Correct Answer: A

Explanation: In Strict Mode, uRPF requires the source IP to match an active FIB route AND the packet must arrive on the exact interface used to reach that source. In Loose Mode, the packet is accepted as long as any valid non-default route to the source exists in the FIB.

[Chapter 14 Practice Question 14.3]

Which Cisco IOS debug command is most critical for troubleshooting TACACS+ or RADIUS authentication failures in real time?

[Chapter 14 Practice Question 14.4]

In IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC), what ICMPv6 message does a client broadcast to discover local routers and obtain network prefix information?

[Chapter 14 Practice Question 14.5]

Which routing protocol authentication method is immune to hash length extension attacks and is recommended on modern Cisco IOS-XE enterprise networks?

Explanation: HMAC-SHA-256 (and SHA-2 family key chains) is cryptographic standard for modern OSPFv2/v3, EIGRP, and BGP routing protocol authentication, providing vastly superior security over legacy MD5.

[Part I: CCNA (200-301) Mock Exam - Question 6]

What port security command prevents a user from connecting a rogue switch and learning more than 3 MAC addresses, shutting down the port if exceeded?
